title: anyone else getting tired of prompt fatigue
author: Middle_Invite_387
selftext: spent all morning tweaking character dailogue and now my brain feels like absolute mush, just gonna close the tab and try again tomorrow

comments.author: florodude
comments.body: This is a common AI phenomenon that I anticipate will get studies at some point.

replies.author: SonderSoft
replies.body:
Generative AI hasn't been available long enough for sufficient research studies; anything you're citing is grasping at straws and likely used half-baked methodology to prove their one-directional thesis.

Coincidentally, many of us are now using generative AI at a moment in our lives where memory retention diminishes.

replies.author: florodude
replies.body: Listen, I'm not an AI hater but these studies are also just common sense and anecdotally I've seen them many times in my workspace and also with myself. Just because AI is only a few years old doesn't mean you can't study it.

replies.author: SonderSoft
replies.body:
I believe it too. Wholeheartedly. But any academic making claims now is putting out indefensible research.

I worry about our future, but also, bad studies are a blight in their own right.

replies.author: florodude
replies.body: I mean that last study is literally [MIT.edu](http://MIT.edu) I suppose you could take it up with them but usually that's a trustworthy source.

comments.author: Sensitive_Day6223
comments.body: Character dialog is essentially text edit, why would you prompt for this?

comments.author: Time_Cat_5212
comments.body: Yeah honestly this work takes a lot of effort.  It's draining.  It's more draining than manual technical work sometimes.  Because of the sheer amount of info you need to synthesize in a short window of time.  It's like switching from bud to shatter lol

replies.author: EchoingAngel
replies.body: It's like being a supervisor on turbo drive because the turnaround is so rapid and the results are less trustworthy, so there's more to check and you NEED to check everything everytime

replies.author: Time_Cat_5212
replies.body: Yeah, except I just don't check everything every time.  I don't want my life to be reduced to checking.  Never been a fan of checking.  I like making.  Making and checking?  Okay.  But if all I'm doing is checking... Man there are other people out there whose brains are suited to that shit.  I'm a creative guy, a problem solver.  I hate review roles.

comments.author: Gugadin_
comments.body:
If you want to try a different workflow, try gamecollab.io, you will be documenting your game instead of writing prompts, and then you can use that documentation as the source of truth through the gamecollab MCP server. You prompt will be to always  synchronize them repo and prompt decisions with the gamecollab project (2 way).

it also allows for collaboration, so one can focus on writing the dialogues and world building while others work on the dialogue system, localization, glossary... everything can connect in a structured way.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: No. I spend so much time doing manual work on the project that I kind of look forward to giving the AI directions. Then it goes off to code something and I go back to creating new assets or reading over code to find issues or whatever else. Consider trying to learn some new things (general game dev concepts, new skills like pixel art or modeling, etc) to mix things up. You don't need to master anything, but just having foundational knowledge will help tremendously and it might feel more like game dev at that point instead of just writing up prompts. But it really depends on what you enjoy. The point of  AI is to do the things you don't enjoy doing. If you don't enjoy doing any part of the process than that would be more an issue with the entire game dev situation that you'd have to think over and resolve.

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
Know when to prompt and when to edit by hand

I think dialogue should be like 90% written by hand, 10% AI review and tweaks

replies.author: FTWGames
replies.body: Agreed. I saved A LOT of back and forth prompting and usage the day I realized I am better off prompting for an in game/sim editor with basic functions so I can manually tweak whatever.

comments.author: Enjoyooooor
comments.body: I get tired after about 14 hours

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
Character dialogue? Of all the things in a game, that's something I'd write by hand!

Let me give you some advice: Gamers get tired of character dialogue much sooner than you get tired of prompting. We usually skip through it. Half-assed dialogue doesn't help immersion.

If you don't like writing it, players sure as shit won't like reading it, or listening to it, either.

Keep it minimal. And write whatever little dialogue there is by hand, to put in as much personal touch as possible. And only give those characters lines that actually matter. Make them memorable.

comments.author: tomqmasters
comments.body: I spend more time on blender when this starts to happen

comments.author: ericoinen
comments.body:
The exhausting part is not the checking, it is that everything arrives in one pile with the same claim on your attention. A line of flavour text and a number that the rest of the game will depend on look identical coming out of the model, so you end up paying the expensive kind of attention to all of it.

The thing that fixed it for me was sorting the output by what a mistake costs. If a wrong result costs nothing, stop checking it, permanently and on purpose. A rock described badly is a rock described badly, you will catch it when you walk past it. If a wrong result is silent and compounds, do not generate it at all. Put it behind code that owns it.

In my case the model narrates and is not allowed to produce a number. Hit points, dice, positions, inventory all live in an engine, and the model receives them and writes around them. It cost me some fluency and the prose is stiffer near those seams. What it bought is that there is no longer a category of output where being wrong is invisible, and my review shrank to reading for taste, which is the part that was enjoyable in the first place.

Applied to your morning specifically: dialogue is the cheap kind. A bad line announces itself the second you read it, it cannot silently poison anything downstream, and the thread is right that it is mostly worth writing by hand anyway. If you spent a whole morning checking it, the loop was pointed at the layer where checking has the least value.
